\chapter{Del --- And Then the List Stops}
\label{ch:del}
\hlchaptermodality{231}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say whose something is, and I know both contractions exist.}

I can say whose something is, and I know both contractions exist.

\section[del]{del — and then the list stops}

\label{lesson:ES-C61-del}



\begin{quote}
\emph{A} + \emph{el} gave you \emph{al}. Now take \emph{de}, which you have had since chapter forty-eight.

Say \emph{de el} quickly, and let the same thing happen.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the second squeeze}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{de} + \emph{el} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{del}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{el libro} \emph{\textbf{del}} \emph{profesor} — the teacher's book
\end{quote}

Same rule, same force. And notice what \emph{del} is doing in that phrase: Spanish has no apostrophe-s, so \emph{of the} is how it says whose something is. \emph{Del profesor} — of the teacher.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Now the part worth celebrating.

\textbf{That is the complete list.} Spanish has exactly \textbf{two} obligatory contractions — \emph{al} and \emph{del} — and no others. Not \emph{de la}, not \emph{a la}, not \emph{de los}. Those stay two words forever.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{a} + \emph{el} & \emph{\textbf{al}} \\
\emph{de} + \emph{el} & \emph{\textbf{del}} \\
\emph{a la}, \emph{de la}, \emph{a los}, \emph{de las} & unchanged \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

It is rare to be handed a grammar rule and told the exceptions are finished. Learn these two and you will never wonder about a third.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{al café}, \emph{del café}
  \item \emph{el libro del profesor}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name both contractions. (\emph{\textbf{Al}} and \emph{\textbf{del}}.)

And how many more are there to learn? (\textbf{None.} That is the whole list.)
\end{tcolorbox}
